_what: Possible patterns: the same kind of thing as the patterns beside them, but ones nobody has proved yet. Each is told as a continuous rundown for a reader new to the subject - what is probably happening, why that is likely, which proved cases sit nearest to it, and what would turn it into cases or knock it down. None of them is evidence. No person or company is named except in the cases already proved.

items.title: The same drafting shops writing the statutes of many governments at once
items.claim: The text of investment, mining and tax laws is probably supplied to many governments from one small set of drafting shops and model texts, so a rule written by a few unelected people is likely in force in countries that never debated it.
items.rule: The copying is measured one level up. A study of more than 600 bilateral investment treaties found the average treaty takes roughly 50 to 65 per cent of its wording from an earlier one, and over 100 copy 80 per cent or more. The map proves the same movement at the level of statutes: industry-written model bills were copied into about 10,000 United States state bills, and a corporate-and-legislator forum drafted an immigration law that was then enacted. Where text travels by copying, the people who wrote the model also advise the ministry that enacts it.
items.conditions: A bill is often drafted by a few people in one ministry or legislative office, with an outside adviser alongside. The adviser's instructions and drafts are not published, and in most countries there is no register of who wrote a bill. Model texts are public; the drafting advice behind each enactment is not.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'ALEC Exposed: 850 corporate-drafted model bills published' and 'Industry-written model bills copied into 10,000 US state bills', both proved. Also 'ALEC meeting drafted Arizona's SB 1070 immigration law', and the Big Four accountants seconded to the Treasury to help write tax law. Nothing proved yet shows one drafting shop supplying the same operative text to several countries.
items.would_show: Two or more national statutes whose operative provisions match one private model, with an engagement letter, secondment record or drafting file showing the same adviser wrote each.
items.would_refute: Ministry drafting files for the closest-matching statutes showing the text was written in-house, with the model used only as a reference and the adviser excluded from drafting.
story: When a country rewrites the law on who owns its minerals, or on what an investor may sue it for, the words are usually typed by a handful of people in one ministry office. Often one of them is not a civil servant at all, but an adviser flown in and paid by a lender, a law firm or an industry body, and he arrives with a draft already written. The probable result is that the same rule, written by people no voter has ever heard of, is in force in dozens of countries that never really debated it.

That text travels is not a guess, because the travelling has been measured. Researchers compared more than 600 investment treaties and found that since 1990 the average one takes between half and two-thirds of its wording straight from an earlier treaty, and over a hundred of them copy eighty per cent or more. This map already holds the same thing happening to ordinary national law. A forum where corporations sat down with state legislators in the United States produced model bills that were copied into roughly ten thousand state bills; 850 of those drafts became public when the operation leaked, and one of its meetings produced the text of Arizona's SB 1070 immigration law.

What keeps it out of sight is that almost nothing about the drafting is published. The model texts are public, the advice is not, and most countries keep no register of who actually wrote a bill, so the adviser's instructions and his successive drafts stay inside the building. The nearest thing this map has already proved at the receiving end is a group of Big Four accountants seconded into a national Treasury to help write tax law: placed inside the body that writes the rule, which is exactly the shape described here.

It would stop being a suspicion the day someone sets two countries' statutes side by side, finds the operative sections matching one private model almost word for word, and produces the engagement letter or secondment record showing the same firm advised both ministries. It would die just as cleanly. If the drafting files for the closest-matching laws showed that civil servants wrote the text themselves and used the model only as a reference, there is nothing here.

items.title: The largest shareholders advising the regulators that oversee them
items.claim: Firms that hold the largest stakes in regulated banks and companies are probably also advising the central banks and finance ministries that set the rules those stakes live under, in several countries at the same time, so one private firm may sit on both sides of the same decision.
items.rule: The structure is documented. One asset manager's advisory arm was created in 2008 to advise governments and central banks, and went on to advise the United States Federal Reserve and several European central banks. Its risk platform was reported to analyse about $21.6 trillion of assets by 2020. Under the Federal Reserve's 2020 facility terms, staff could move from that work to client-facing work after a two-week cooling-off period. The map proves the same arrangement elsewhere: a founder of a finance firm was given a desk inside a government department while the firm was in dealings with it.
items.conditions: These engagements are often awarded without open competition and the contracts are not published. Members of the United States Congress asked in 2020 for the contract terms and conflict-of-interest procedures. The information the adviser sees, such as bank balance sheets under supervisory review or an intervention before it is announced, reaches no other market participant. The safeguards are set and audited by the firm itself.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Greensill Capital: founder inside Downing Street, civil servant on its side', and 'Banker offered Puerto Rico's governor campaign cash to replace his regulator', both proved. Nothing proved yet ties an asset manager's advisory work to a decision that moved its own holdings.
items.would_show: A supervisory, purchase or intervention decision where the record shows the adviser's own holdings or products were affected and its staff drafted or recommended the option chosen.
items.would_refute: Contracts and internal access logs showing the information barriers held, with no traffic between the advisory team and the investment side on the decisions at issue.
story: A small number of asset managers now hold a slice of nearly every large bank and listed company in the world. The same firms are also hired, for a fee, to advise the central banks and finance ministries that decide the rules those holdings live under. The probable position is that in several countries at once a single private firm sits on both sides of the same decision: it owns the thing being regulated, and it is in the room helping to write the regulation.

The structure is not hidden. One asset manager set up an arm in 2008 for the specific purpose of advising governments and central banks, and it went on to advise the United States Federal Reserve and a series of European central banks; by 2020 its risk software was reported to be analysing around twenty-one trillion dollars of assets. When the Federal Reserve ran an emergency corporate credit programme that year, the published terms allowed the firm's staff to move from that work back to serving its own clients after a two-week pause.

What makes it workable is the paperwork nobody sees. These jobs have repeatedly been handed out without open competition and the contracts have not been published; members of Congress wrote in 2020 to ask for the terms and the conflict-of-interest rules and did not get them. The adviser meanwhile sees things no other investor sees, such as the state of a bank's books under supervisory review, or the design of an intervention before it is announced. The barriers that are supposed to contain that information are set by the firm and audited by the firm.

This map has already proved the smaller version twice over: the founder of a finance company given a desk inside Downing Street with a civil servant working on the company's side, and a banker in Puerto Rico offering the governor campaign money to replace his own regulator. What is missing is one decision — a supervisory call, a purchase, a rescue — where the record shows the adviser's own holdings were among those affected and its staff recommended the option chosen. Produce the access logs showing no traffic between the advisory desk and the trading desk on those decisions, and the suspicion is answered.

items.title: Companies voting the technical standards that become law
items.claim: In the technical committees whose texts national law then adopts by reference, the voting experts are probably in large part employed by the firms the standard governs, so rules with the force of law are likely drafted by the industries they bind.
items.rule: The map proves the mechanism at a standards body. Partners of a software maker joined national committees to vote its document format into the international standard, and a national intelligence agency steered a weakened encryption standard through the standards bodies. The bodies are open to industry by design, and their texts become binding when a government adopts them by reference. A committee that no government controls, whose text becomes law, is the same shape as a lobbyist drafting a bill, which the map proves elsewhere.
items.conditions: Committees run to a few dozen members and are staffed through national standards bodies, many funded by selling the standards they help write. The employer of each voting member, and who paid for each delegate, is generally not stated in the published standard. Drafts and ballots go to members, not to the public.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Microsoft partners joined national committees to vote its format into ISO' and 'NSA steered a weakened encryption standard through NIST and ISO', both proved. Nothing proved yet ties a standard to a member's employer in a way that decided the outcome.
items.would_show: A standard later adopted into national law where the committee record shows the drafting members were employed by firms whose product the text admits or excludes, and a competitor's objection was voted down by those members.
items.would_refute: Committee rosters and ballot records showing government, academic and consumer members held the deciding votes on the standards in question.
story: Most people never learn how a technical standard becomes law. A government writes a single line into its rulebook saying that equipment, or a building, or a medical device must meet standard number such-and-such, and from that moment the text of a private committee has the force of law. The committees that write those texts are open to the industries they govern, and the probable position is that the people holding the votes are in large part employed by the firms the standard is meant to bind.

This map has already proved it twice inside the same bodies. A software maker's commercial partners joined national standards committees and voted its document format through to international adoption. Separately, a national intelligence agency steered a deliberately weakened encryption standard through the standards process, which is the same mechanism turned to a different purpose: get your people into the committee and the committee's output carries your preference out into everyone else's law.

The conditions favour it. A committee may be a few dozen people and a working group fewer. Participation runs through national standards bodies, many of which are funded by selling the very standards they help write. The employer of each voting member is generally not printed in the published standard, drafts and ballots circulate only to members, and the finished text is usually sold rather than published, so the public pays to read a rule it is bound by.

To turn this into a case you would need a standard later written into national law, with a committee record showing that the members who drafted it worked for the firms whose product the text lets in or keeps out, and a competitor's objection voted down by those same members. The honest refutation is just as available: publish the rosters and the ballots, and if government, academic and consumer members held the deciding votes, this pattern is wrong.

items.title: The judges and advocates of investment disputes being one circle
items.claim: The tribunals that decide whether a state may regulate an investor are probably staffed largely from a small circle of people who also argue cases before the same tribunals, so the judges and the advocates in this system may be substantially the same people.
items.rule: This is counted, not supposed. A survey of 1,077 investment arbitrations found 509, or 47 per cent, involved arbitrators who were at the same time acting as counsel or expert in other cases. The system's own rule-writers treat the overlap as a defect: the UNCITRAL working group agreed a code of conduct in 2023 with cooling-off periods of one to three years. The map proves that arbitration itself is a place where influence is bought: a company bribed a government lawyer during an arbitration.
items.conditions: A tribunal is three people, one chosen by each side and one agreed between them, drawn from a small pool of repeat appointees and paid by the parties. Hearings and many awards are confidential. Until the 2023 code, disclosure of concurrent roles was left largely to the arbitrator.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'P&ID bribed a Nigerian government lawyer during arbitration', and 'Leaks say arbitrators weighed bribery of Kazakh officials over Karacha', both proved as bribery in arbitration rather than as double-hatting. Honest gap: no proved case of an arbitrator with concurrent roles shaping an award.
items.would_show: An award where an arbitrator was concurrently counsel for a party, or for its affiliate, in another case on the same treaty provision, and did not disclose it at the time.
items.would_refute: Disclosure records across the same case set showing concurrent roles were declared, and party challenges were heard and ruled on in the closest cases.
story: A company that dislikes a country's new law can, under thousands of investment treaties, sue that country for compensation. The case is not heard in a public court. It goes to a tribunal of three private individuals, one chosen by each side and one agreed between them, and they can order a state to pay hundreds of millions. The probable position is that the people who sit as judges in this system are drawn from the same small circle of lawyers who argue the cases, so that the bench and the bar are substantially the same few dozen people.

This one has been counted rather than guessed at. A survey of 1,077 investment arbitrations found that 509 of them, forty-seven per cent, involved an arbitrator who was at the same time acting as counsel or as a paid expert in other cases. The people who run the system treat the overlap as a defect, not a theory: a United Nations working group agreed a code of conduct in 2023 imposing cooling-off periods of one to three years, and some newer treaties ban the practice outright.

Everything about the setting protects it. Appointments are repeat business from a small pool, the parties pay the arbitrators' fees, hearings and many awards are confidential, and until that 2023 code it was largely left to the arbitrator himself to disclose what else he was working on.

Here the map has to be honest about what it holds. It proves that arbitration is a place where influence gets bought — a company bribed a Nigerian government lawyer during an arbitration, and leaked material describes arbitrators weighing the bribery of Kazakh officials in a dispute over the Karachaganak field — but it holds no case of an arbitrator's second hat shaping an award. That is what would be needed: an award where the arbitrator was at the same time counsel for a party or its affiliate in another case on the same treaty clause, and did not say so. If the disclosure records across those cases show the second roles were declared and the resulting challenges heard, the pattern fails.

items.title: Suppliers and private funders holding seats over what global health buys
items.claim: The bodies that set global health priorities and buy vaccines at scale are probably giving governing seats and funding leverage to the suppliers and private funders who gain from what is bought, so part of the purchaser's agenda may be set by the sellers.
items.rule: The arrangement is published and can be read from the budget. More than 80 per cent of the World Health Organization's budget is voluntary money, and in 2024 to 2025 the largest contributor was a private foundation at about 13 per cent of that. A vaccine alliance was second at about 11.6 per cent, and its board gives permanent seats to the same foundation and to the vaccine industry. The map already proves tobacco companies working inside the WHO. This is the purchasing layer of the same arrangement.
items.conditions: Priorities are set by boards of a few dozen people deciding by consensus or two-thirds majority. Where a body depends on one donor for a large share of its money, withdrawal is a sanction that needs no vote. Supply agreements, prices and volume commitments are routinely confidential.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Tobacco companies secretly worked to undermine WHO from inside', proved as industry inside a rule-making body. Nothing proved yet ties a board seat to a purchase decision.
items.would_show: A procurement or priority decision where the record shows a board member's own product was selected and that member took part in the vote.
items.would_refute: Board minutes and recusal records showing industry and funder seats were excluded from votes on the products they supply.
story: The bodies that decide which vaccines and medicines the poorer half of the world receives, and that buy them by the hundred million dose, are not funded the way people assume. The probable position is that the suppliers who sell the product and the private funders who pay for it also hold seats at the table where it is decided what gets bought, which would put part of the buyer's agenda in the hands of the sellers.

This can be read straight off the budget. More than eighty per cent of the World Health Organization's money is voluntary contributions rather than dues, and in the 2024 to 2025 budget the single largest contributor was a private foundation at about thirteen per cent of that voluntary money. A vaccine alliance was the second largest at around eleven and a half per cent, and that alliance's own board hands permanent seats to the same foundation and allocated seats to the vaccine industry.

The leverage does not need a vote to work. Priorities are set by boards of a few dozen people deciding by consensus or two-thirds majority, and where an organisation depends on one donor for a large slice of its budget, the mere possibility of withdrawal shapes what gets proposed. The supply agreements, the prices paid and the volumes committed are routinely confidential, so the public cannot check what its money bought.

The map already proves that an industry can work inside this institution: tobacco companies were found to have operated inside the WHO to undermine it. What has not been shown is the purchasing version — a procurement or priority decision where the record shows a board member's own product was selected and that member took part in the decision. Board minutes and recusal records showing industry and funder seats were kept out of votes on their own products would settle it the other way.

items.title: Central bankers and the banks they supervise meeting in closed rooms
items.claim: Decisions on money and bank supervision are probably shaped in invitation-only forums where the officials who take them and the bankers they supervise meet without published minutes, moving part of policy out of any record the public can reach.
items.rule: An official watchdog has already found this kind of overlap improper. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman found that a central bank president's membership of an invitation-only bankers' club amounted to maladministration, because members included directors of banks the bank supervised. She recommended he suspend the membership and that future presidents not join. The map proves the older form: bankers secretly drafted the Federal Reserve plan at Jekyll Island, and bank owners bribed a central bank chief in Latvia.
items.conditions: Membership is by invitation and meetings are confidential. Attendance may appear in an official diary, but agendas, papers and discussion do not. The firms in the room are often the ones whose capital, resolution and liquidity support the officials decide.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Bankers secretly drafted the Federal Reserve plan at Jekyll Island', and 'Latvian bank's owners bribed central bank chief and ECB member', both proved. Honest gap: no proved case of a closed-forum meeting shaping a specific rate or supervisory decision.
items.would_show: A supervisory or policy position that changed after a closed meeting, with notes, correspondence or testimony tying the change to what was said there.
items.would_refute: Published agendas and summaries showing the meetings dealt only in general analysis, with matters concerning members' own firms excluded.
story: Decisions about interest rates, and about which banks are sound enough to carry on, are taken by a very small number of officials. Some of those officials belong to invitation-only forums where they sit, in private and without published minutes, alongside executives of the banks they supervise. The probable position is that part of monetary and supervisory policy is shaped in those rooms, where no record exists that the public can ever reach.

An official watchdog has already called this improper. In January 2018 the European Ombudsman concluded that a central bank president's membership of one such invitation-only bankers' club amounted to maladministration, precisely because its members included directors of banks that his institution supervised. She recommended that he give up the membership and that his successors never take it up.

The map holds the older and blunter forms of the same thing. The plan that became the Federal Reserve was drafted in secret by bankers on Jekyll Island, at a meeting arranged to look like a duck-shooting trip. In Latvia, the owners of a bank bribed the central bank governor, who also sat on the European Central Bank's council. The modern version needs no bribe, because the banker and the supervisor are already in the same room by invitation.

What is missing is the link between a meeting and an outcome: a supervisory or policy position that changed after one of these gatherings, with notes, correspondence or testimony tying the change to what was said there. Publish the agendas and summaries, show the discussions stayed on general analysis and that matters touching members' own banks were excluded, and this one is dead.

items.title: The firms that sell tax structures writing the laws that allow them
items.claim: In jurisdictions that supply secrecy and tax residence to the rest of the world, statutes are probably written in large part by the private firms that then sell the structures those statutes permit, so the law may be drafted by its own customers.
items.rule: Legal scholarship describes interested private parties working closely with the legislatures of small offshore jurisdictions, partners of offshore firms holding government posts, and jurisdictions converting lawmaking authority into revenue. Leak-based reporting found that more than 300 lawyers at one global firm had advised a state or international body on tax or anti-corruption legislation, while the firm was connected to more than 440 offshore companies. The map proves the same pairing in a different setting: accounting-firm staff seconded to a national Treasury to help write tax law.
items.conditions: A small legislature may have no standing drafting office, so an outside draft is often the only draft. The instructing client and fee are not published. The firm that drafts may also incorporate and administer the entities the statute creates, so one firm writes the rule and sells the product.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Big Four accountants seconded to the Treasury to help write tax law', proved as placement inside the body that writes the rule. Honest gap: no proved case of an offshore firm drafting the statute under which it then sells structures.
items.would_show: A statute or amendment whose drafting file, legislative record or billing shows a private firm wrote it, where that firm also sells the structures the statute enables.
items.would_refute: Drafting records showing the text came from a government law office or a multilateral adviser with no commercial interest in the structures created.
story: A dozen small jurisdictions supply the rest of the world with secrecy, shell companies and tax residence. Their company and trust laws are unusually well built for that trade. The probable explanation is that those laws are largely written by the private firms that then sell the structures the laws permit, which would mean the statute book of these places is drafted by its own customers.

Some firms say so themselves: legislative drafting is listed as a practice area by the largest law firm in at least one such jurisdiction, alongside trusts, funds and company administration. Leaked records showed that more than three hundred lawyers at a single global firm had advised a government or an international body on tax or anti-corruption legislation, while that same firm was connected to more than four hundred offshore companies. Academic work on these places describes interested private parties working hand in hand with tiny legislatures, firm partners holding seats in government, and small states turning the power to make law into a revenue stream.

The mechanics are mundane. A legislature of a few dozen members may have no permanent drafting office, so an outside draft is not merely welcome, it is the only draft. Who instructed the drafter and what he was paid are not published. And the firm that writes the rule frequently also incorporates the companies, administers the trusts and acts as registered agent, so one set of partners writes the law, sells the product and keeps the records.

The nearest thing already proved here is accounting-firm staff seconded into a national Treasury to help write tax law. To close the gap you would need a statute or amendment whose drafting file, legislative record or billing shows a private firm wrote it, where that firm also sells the structures it enables. Drafting records showing the text came from a government law office, or from an adviser with no commercial stake in the structures created, would clear it.

items.title: Former intelligence officers selling their service's methods to foreign clients
items.claim: Former officers of national intelligence services are probably working for foreign states and private clients in numbers large enough to matter, carrying the access and methods of the services they left.
items.rule: One case is proved in the form of a United States prosecution agreement. Three former intelligence and military employees ran hacking operations for a foreign government through a company from 2016 to 2019, paid $1.685 million between them, surrendered their clearances and accepted employment limits. Enforcement officials then warned other former employees publicly, which implies the pool is larger than the three charged. The map proves the state-to-state form of the same thing: a state's own service running the access it holds.
items.conditions: These engagements are commercial contracts with non-disclosure terms. Export control is the main legal handle, and it reaches tools more readily than people. There is no public register of where former officers of most services go. The client can classify the work it commissions.
items.documented: Honest zero. The map holds no case of former officers selling their service's methods to a foreign client. Nearest proved: 'CIA and BND secretly owned Swiss cipher firm Crypto AG', which shows a service inside a commercial vendor. The rule above rests on the public prosecution record outside the map.
items.would_show: A second state's enforcement action or court record showing former officers of its own service worked for a foreign client against its interests or its allies.
items.would_refute: Post-employment records showing former officers' foreign work was licensed and supervised, leaving the case isolated rather than typical.
story: A government trains someone for years to break into other people's systems, run informants and read other states' mail. Then that person resigns. The skills, the methods and the contacts leave with him, and there is a market. The probable position is that former officers of national intelligence services are now working for foreign governments and private clients in numbers large enough to matter.

One instance is proved, and its shape is general. In 2021 the United States settled with three men who had served in its intelligence community or military and had then spent the years from 2016 to 2019 running hacking operations for a foreign government through a private company. They paid just under 1.7 million dollars between them, surrendered every security clearance they held and accepted limits on who they may work for. What matters as much as the case is what officials did next: they issued a public warning aimed at other former employees, which is not the act of people who believe they have found all of it.

The trade is protected by its paperwork. These are commercial contracts under foreign law with confidentiality clauses. Export control is the main legal handle and it grips tools far better than it grips people. There is no public register of where former officers of most services end up, and the client is a state that can classify the work it has commissioned.

Here the map holds nothing, and says so. Its nearest case is the mirror image rather than the thing itself: the CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned Crypto AG, the Swiss firm that sold cipher machines to around a hundred governments, and read what those governments wrote — a service hidden inside a company, rather than a company staffed by a service's alumni. What would turn this into a case is a second country's prosecution or court record showing its own former officers collecting against it, or against its allies, for a foreign client. Post-employment records showing such work is licensed and supervised service by service would leave the 2021 case an outlier rather than a sample.

items.title: Suppliers of national identity and payment systems inside the bodies that choose them
items.claim: The companies that build national identity and payment systems are probably inside the ministries and programmes that choose and mandate those systems, so a few suppliers may set the terms on which large populations are enrolled, identified and paid.
items.rule: The map proves the purchasing end of this repeatedly. A multinational paid over $100 million to officials for a $1 billion ID-card deal, and contractors paid a national legislative leader. A Belgian firm was sent to trial over a cut of each passport issued in one country. Identity systems have few qualified bidders, and the lender programmes that fund them publish technical guidance that names vendor lock-in as a risk in borrowing countries.
items.conditions: A national identity decision is usually taken by one commission or ministry, under a single integrator contract running for years. Biometric matching, card supply and payment switching each have few qualified bidders. Contract terms, pricing and data-ownership clauses are often unpublished.
items.documented: Nearest on the map: 'Siemens paid over $100m to Argentine officials for a $1bn ID-card deal', and 'e-KTP contractors paid Indonesia's House Speaker Setya Novanto', both proved as bribery in procurement. Honest gap: no proved case of a supplier writing the specification it then wins.
items.would_show: An identity or payment mandate where the specification was written by a bidder, or the deciding official was employed by one before or after the award.
items.would_refute: Procurement files for the largest such programmes showing specifications written in-house and competitive awards, with deciding officials unconnected to any bidder.
story: Across much of the world a person's ability to vote, be treated, cross a border or be paid a benefit now runs through one national identity system and one payment rail. A handful of companies build them. The probable position is that those companies are inside the ministries and programmes that choose the systems and then make them compulsory, which would let a few suppliers set the terms on which whole populations are enrolled, identified and paid.

The buying end of this is proved on the map repeatedly. A multinational paid more than a hundred million dollars to officials to win a one-billion-dollar national identity card contract in Argentina. Contractors on Indonesia's electronic identity card paid the Speaker of its parliament. A Belgian firm was sent to trial over taking a cut of every passport issued in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The pattern here is the step beyond bribery: not paying for the contract, but being inside the body that writes what the contract must contain.

The conditions are ideal for it. One commission or ministry usually decides, under a single integrator contract that runs for years and then renews. Worldwide there are few credible bidders for biometric matching, card production or payment switching, so the shortlist is short before anyone writes a specification. Contract terms, unit prices and the clauses saying who owns the data often go unpublished. The lenders funding these programmes name vendor lock-in as a risk in their own guidance, having watched it happen.

What is not yet shown is a mandate where the technical specification was written by a bidder, or where the official who made the decision worked for one before or after the award. Procurement files for the largest of these programmes showing specifications written in-house, competitive awards and deciding officials with no connection to any bidder would refute it.
